analysis.one_liner: Requires companies and agencies to tell people when hackers steal their personal data.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, received a single subcommittee hearing in November 2003, and died without a committee vote or floor action when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill, modeled on California's 2002 data breach law, would have required any federal agency or company in interstate commerce that holds electronic records to tell people when their unencrypted Social Security number, driver's license number, or financial account information was acquired by an unauthorized person. Notice had to come promptly, with narrow delays allowed for law enforcement investigations. The Federal Trade Commission could fine violators up to $5,000 per violation, and state attorneys general could sue on behalf of residents to recover money. The bill would have replaced most state breach-notification laws with this federal standard, keeping California's rules in place, but it never reached a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyday people whose banks, employers, agencies, or retailers hold their personal information. Breach notices give them the chance to freeze their credit, change passwords, and monitor accounts before identity thieves monetize stolen Social Security numbers and account numbers. State attorneys general also gain a federal tool to win restitution for residents.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers whose personal data is breached

how_it_helps.text: Requires any agency or company holding electronic records to notify every U.S. resident whose unencrypted personal information — Social Security number, driver's license number, or financial account number — was, or was reasonably believed to have been, taken by an unauthorized person.
Requires notice to come as expediently as possible and without unreasonable delay, so people can freeze their credit, change passwords, and watch their accounts before thieves use the data.

Backs the requirement with fines of up to $5,000 per violation ($25,000 per day), FTC enforcement, and the power for state attorneys general to sue for restitution and compensation on behalf of their residents.
Lets law enforcement delay notification only while needed to protect a criminal investigation, preventing companies from using open investigations as an open-ended excuse to stay quiet.

analysis.who_pays: Federal agencies and companies engaged in interstate commerce that hold consumer data — banks, retailers, data brokers, and others. They bear the cost of detecting breaches and sending notifications, plus fines up to $5,000 per violation and exposure to state attorney general lawsuits.
analysis.who_pays_short: Companies and agencies holding consumer data

drawbacks.text: The bill would have superseded state breach-notification laws nationwide — preserving only California's — which could have replaced stronger state protections with a lower federal standard and left consumers in most states with one-size-fits-all rules.

Financial institutions get a major carve-out: a bank is deemed compliant if it runs a security program that blocks unauthorized transactions and notifies customers only after fraud actually occurs — meaning customers might never learn their data was taken if no charges went through.
Penalties are modest: a maximum fine of $5,000 per violation, capped at $25,000 per day, with no private right of individual damages beyond what state AGs could win on residents' behalf.

For large breaches, companies could avoid contacting individuals and instead use email, website postings, or media notices once more than 500,000 people were affected or direct notice cost over $250,000.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and proven in the state it was modeled on: prompt notice lets people freeze credit, change passwords, and watch accounts before thieves strike. The costs are compliance spending by data-holding companies and some useless paperwork for large breaches where substitute notice reaches no one personally. The bill's bigger design problems run the other way: the banking carve-out could leave customers uninformed about breaches the bank already detected, and the preemption of state laws (California's excepted) could have replaced tougher state rules with a lower federal floor. A stronger bill would have required notice in more circumstances and left state laws intact.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee after a single subcommittee hearing in November 2003 and never got a committee vote or a floor vote before Congress adjourned.

narrative.text: Feinstein introduced the bill on June 26, 2003, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor during the two years the bill was pending.

The only further action was a hearing before the Judiciary Subcommittee on Terrorism, Technology and Homeland Security on November 4, 2003; the full committee never reported the bill, so the Senate never debated or voted on it.
The 108th Congress ended January 3, 2005, and the bill expired with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies and agencies holding Americans' personal data — they faced no new notification duties, fines, or state lawsuits. Consumers were left to rely on the patchwork of state breach laws that had sprung up outside Congress.

for.name: Sen. Dianne Feinstein
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 26, 2003 and delivered introductory remarks; it was her first and only action on the measure in this Congress.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee, held one hearing in November 2003, and never reported it out for a Senate vote.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill attracted zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split is visible in the record.

industries.note: The bill imposed new notification duties on banks, but Section 3(a)(6) let them avoid customer notice entirely if they ran a fraud-blocking security program and only notified after actual unauthorized transactions — a compliance regime examined by their existing federal regulators. The carve-out spares them the reputational cost of breach disclosures.

industries.industry: Companies holding consumer data (retailers, data brokers, credit bureaus, federal agencies)
industries.note: Any organization with Americans' names plus Social Security, driver's license, or financial account numbers would have had to detect breaches, notify affected people quickly, and face FTC fines and state attorney general lawsuits. Compliance costs and breach publicity are the price; consumers get the information they need to protect themselves.

industries.industry: Identity theft protection and credit monitoring services
industries.note: Breach notifications are the main trigger for consumers to buy credit monitoring and identity-theft services, so a national notification standard would have enlarged this market alongside the protection it gave consumers.
